116	## For builders
117	
118	Everything above is the whole job for a customer. What follows is for a programmer. Maybe you want to see what the setup walk does, or run a piece of it by hand. Maybe you want to wire the gate into CI, or drive the documents directly instead of going through the agent.
119	
120	### The technical walk-throughs
121	
122	[`docs/adoption.md`](docs/adoption.md) explains the setup walk step 2 runs. The normative procedures it follows are [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) for an existing codebase and [`adopt/START.md`](adopt/START.md) for an empty directory.
123	
124	### The push gate, by hand
125	
126	The four checks below are what a host project gets from the scaffold, at `scaffold/guardrails/` in this tree. This repository's own pre-push hook predates the scaffold, and runs a larger, differently organized check set of its own, named in [`guardrails/README.md`](guardrails/README.md). The four checks above are not additionally vendored into this repository's `guardrails/` under these names.
127	
128	Three things have to be true before any of it works, and each has one command that says so. `python3 --version` must print 3.9 or newer; install a newer Python if it does not. `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` must print `true` in your project's root; run `git init` there if it does not. And `git rev-parse --verify origin/main` must name a commit. The tests-present check diffs your work against that ref. If the command fails, you name your own base in the config instead, two paragraphs down. It fails on a project with no remote, and on one whose default branch is named otherwise. All of this assumes Claude Code on your machine: the pack is a set of skills it loads, and step 2 happens inside it.
129	
130	By hand, run one script from your project's root. It lives in the pack tree you already got in step 1, so the line you type depends on which road you took:
131	
132	```
133	# plugin road — the tree sits in the plugin cache
134	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
135	
136	# clone road — the tree is the clone from step 1
137	bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
138	```
139	
140	It writes six files into your project's `guardrails/`: the four checks, the shared library they load, and a copy of the page that documents them. It seeds `guardrails.config.json` when your project carries none, and it never overwrites a config you already filled. It also writes `scripts/ratchet-manifest.json`, creating a `scripts/` folder if you have none. A good run prints one `vendored:` line per file and a `seeded:` line for the config. Then it prints the manual steps that remain, and ends on a line reading `{"severity": "ok", "code": "scaffold-install", ...}`.
141	
142	That config then needs two things from you. Fill in your paths: the spec, the test matrix, the queue, the tests, and the surface registry. The registry is the table listing every surface the project ships. A surface is one named part a user meets: a screen, a page, a command, a public function. The queue is the dated list of what has been asked of the product and where each ask stands. This repository keeps its own in [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md).
143	
144	Three more fields in that same config decide what the checks can see. The seeded example fills them with values a fresh project rarely matches. `user_facing_globs` names the files whose change demands a test. `rendered_artifacts`, or `render_command` instead, names what the completeness check reads as your shipped output. `surface_discovery_pattern` is the expression that finds surface ids inside that output. Leave the first two as they ship and two of the four checks go red on a path that does not exist. Leave the pattern matching nothing your artifacts contain and the check passes while seeing nothing. That is the one failure that never announces itself — see "Known issues" below for where this repository's own config still ships that way. The setup walk in step 2 fills this config for you, from what your project ships. This paragraph is for a programmer editing it by hand instead.
145	
146	One field more, `base_ref`, decides what the tests-present check compares your work against when `origin/main` does not resolve. That means a project with no remote, or one whose default branch is named otherwise. Set it to your own base branch, `"base_ref": "main"`, and that check has its ground. Leave it out on such a project. The second line of the push gate then reds: `no base ref to diff against`. That line is `check_tests_present.py`. [`scaffold/guardrails/README.md`](scaffold/guardrails/README.md) describes every field one at a time.
147	
148	Second, empty the config's `waivers` block, so the line reads `"waivers": {}`. It ships holding one example waiver, and that example switches the completeness check off. Every run prints `WAIVED (completeness): no rendered artifact yet — declared 2026-07-10, owner <maintainer>` and exits zero. The line is loud enough. What it says is that someone else's declaration, dated before you arrived, stands where your own would go. Until you empty the block, you run on three checks instead of four.
149	
150	One more step, outside the config: add these four lines to `.git/hooks/pre-push`.
151	
152	```sh
153	python3 guardrails/check_completeness.py || exit 1
154	python3 guardrails/check_tests_present.py || exit 1
155	python3 guardrails/check_traces_to_spec.py || exit 1
156	python3 guardrails/check_conflicts.py || exit 1
157	```
158	
159	Create that file if your project has none, and make it executable with `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push`. Run it once by hand with `sh .git/hooks/pre-push`, then `echo $?` to see the exit code. Four lines each opening `OK (` and a `0` mean the gate is live. The same four lines are in your own `guardrails/README.md`, the copy the script just vendored, on either road. Those hook lines take no arguments, so the `--base <ref>` flag the checks accept is for running one by hand. What the hook itself reads is `origin/main`, or the `base_ref` you set in the config. The setup walk writes this same hook file for you. This step is for a programmer who would rather write it themselves. It is also the step for wiring the gate into CI instead of `.git/hooks/`.
160	
161	Two more installers finish the gate the adoption procedure asks for. Both run from your project's root, out of the same pack tree as before:
162	
163	```
164	# plugin road
165	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-ratchet.sh
166	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/scripts/install-pack-hooks.sh
167	
168	# clone road
169	bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-ratchet.sh
170	bash /path/to/live-spec/scripts/install-pack-hooks.sh
171	```
172	
173	The first vendors the style, redundancy, and freeze gates. It measures your documents as they stand today and writes the debt caps at those numbers. It generates `tests/test_ratchet_lock.py`, so the gate is green the day it lands and the debt can only hold or shrink from there. It ends by printing a fifth gate line for your push hook. That line belongs in the same `.git/hooks/pre-push` you just wrote, beside the four. Write it as `python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_ratchet_lock.py || exit 1`. The printed form ends `|| fail=1`, which fits a hook that collects every failure before it exits. The recipe labels it `gate r`. This repository's own hook set already gives that letter to a different check, so give yours another label if you carry that set.
174	
175	The second puts the pack's own scan hooks on your machine, and this one reaches outside your project. It copies the hook files under `~/.claude/hooks/` and writes their wiring into `~/.claude/settings.json`, which every project of yours reads. Run it with `--dry-run` first: it prints every file and every line it would add, and touches nothing. Running it for real twice changes nothing, and your personal overlay files are never written by it. [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) counts both installers as part of the attach. The setup walk runs both of these for you too; they are here for a programmer setting a project up outside a live-spec session.
176	
177	### What the spec looks like
178	
179	A project under the pack keeps one document, `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, stating what the product promises today. A stranger can read a section on the first pass. The format is a requirements genre, defined in [`docs/spec-format.md`](docs/spec-format.md):
180	
181	- The document opens with a **glossary**. Every domain noun used anywhere in the spec has a one-sentence definition. An ordinary English word needs no entry.
182	- The body is a list of **requirements**. Each requirement has a short **context** (when the situation arises, who is involved, what the reader sees), one **user story** (as a person in a named role, I want one thing, so that one benefit follows), and **acceptance criteria**.
183	- The criteria are grouped into **named cases**. A case names a situation and lists two to six numbered steps. Each step carries one trigger and one response, written with the plain keywords *when*, *while*, *if*, *then*, and *shall*.
184	- Each line ends with a short code in brackets: `[INV-104]`, or `[E-6, T-12]` where several apply. The code is that rule's permanent id, and this spec line is its home. The test matrix and the architecture document cite the same code, so a maintainer can walk between all three. A reader can ignore the codes.
185	
186	A **fact** is one thing the spec says the product does. The test matrix follows the same format, defined in [`docs/test-matrix-format.md`](docs/test-matrix-format.md). Each matrix row takes one fact and states both halves of it: what it does, and what it must never do. Rows are grouped by architecture node, and the coverage table at the document's end is generated from the rows and gated against hand edits.
187	
188	The roadmap and the architecture document follow the format too. The architecture is defined in [`docs/architecture-format.md`](docs/architecture-format.md). Each part of the system stands as one node section, naming its responsibility, the facts it owns, and where it lives in the code. One shared parser reads every node section, and every check reads a node through it.
189	
190	Work enters the spec before code. A new behaviour arrives as a spec change, gets reviewed, and only then gets built. A guardrail check goes red when a shipped behaviour has no spec sentence behind it. A removed feature leaves a dated tombstone, and its history moves to `JOURNAL.md`.
191	
192	### What's different
193	
194	**The gates are scripts.** Four checks decide whether a push in your project is allowed. The surface registry is the table listing the surfaces a project ships, `SURFACES.md` here. The first check reads that table both ways round: everything the registry lists is really shipped, and everything shipped is listed. The second: a change to a user-facing file carries a test. The third: every listed surface cites a spec code that exists. The fourth: no code is claimed twice and no surface is registered twice. The four are Python on the pre-push hook, mirrored in [CI](.github/workflows/gates.yml). That is what a host project's own hook runs. This repository's own pre-push hook is older than the scaffold. It runs a larger, differently named roster of its own, listed in [`guardrails/README.md`](guardrails/README.md). A change that has drifted from its specification is refused. Some other frameworks enforce their specs by asking a model to check. A model having a bad day reports that it checked.
195	
196	**It can decline a gate it cannot build honestly, and records the reasoning.** One planned gate was refused. It would have gone red on a session that landed two independent pieces of work one after the other. Those two could have run side by side. The [record of that refusal](docs/prover/2026-07-18-rows386-412-414-lane-open-act.md) gives three reasons. Whether two pieces of work were independent is a senior's read, and a script sees only a diff. The evidence a correct run leaves is destroyed on purpose: a finished lane's branch is torn down when it lands. And the one signal a script could key on would fire on every lawful one-at-a-time run too. So the requirement shipped as a written discipline, held by the session and backed by no script. The rule behind that: a requirement no script can enforce stays a note, and a judgment call is never wired as an automated gate. The records are in [`docs/prover/`](docs/prover/), including the ones where the reviewer missed something and said so.
197	
198	**The rules are built for a model's failure modes.** Every claim shown for review is tagged with its source. The source is the artifact it was read from, your own recorded word, or the agent's inference. Inferences are flagged loudest ([the rule](skills/communicator/SKILL.md)). The line between what a document says and what a model filled in is invisible to a reader, and that is where the errors live. A background worker from a dead session counts as a live writer until three signals agree it stopped. Its files stop changing, its heartbeat goes stale, and it fails to answer a direct message ([`docs/worker-liveness.md`](docs/worker-liveness.md)). A decision you withdraw twice keeps its recommendation and is never raised again, because a tireless agent will go on asking ([the rule](skills/communicator/SKILL.md)).
199	
200	### The gates stabilize first
201	
202	Only the mechanical gates are checked independently. A judgment call — the model reviewing its own work — has no independent check of its own. That is why the gates are built as scripts.
203	
204	The gates stabilize first. Each one carries a red-first proof. Before a gate existed, someone watched the exact failure it now catches. They watched it happen for real, on purpose — that is what shows the gate can actually fail, not only pass. Every gate's proof is named in [`guardrails/gate-red-proofs.json`](guardrails/gate-red-proofs.json). A gate with no proof blocks the push.
205	
206	### The skills
207	
208	[`live-spec-base`](skills/live-spec-base/) holds the shared rulebook · [`build-pipeline`](skills/build-pipeline/) sequences a change end to end · [`spec-author`](skills/spec-author/) writes the living spec · [`product-prover`](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover) reviews it (external skill, own repository) · [`product-prover-pack`](skills/product-prover-pack/) is the adapter that binds that external skill to this pack · [`design-reviewer`](skills/design-reviewer/) asks whether the design itself is right once the spec holds together · [`test-author`](skills/test-author/) derives the matrix and the tests · [`communicator`](skills/communicator/) shows work and asks answerable questions · [`feedback-intake`](skills/feedback-intake/) routes what you hand back · [`feedback-collector`](skills/feedback-collector/) sends upstream notes with your consent · [`text-audit`](skills/text-audit/) reads a text as a stranger and fixes where they stop · [`publish`](skills/publish/) gates anything leaving the machine.
209	
210	### External skills
211	
212	- **[product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover)** — spec verification and
213	  validation with formal-verification thinking. The pack's review step invokes it; it lives in its
214	  own repository with its own version line. `scripts/install-external-skills.sh` installs it
215	  (version floor in `skills/product-prover-pack/SKILL.md`); the pack-side bindings — mode names,
216	  record contract, pin map — live on that same page.
217	
218	The ideas in five minutes: [`OVERVIEW.md`](OVERVIEW.md) · [pipeline](docs/pipeline.md) · [adoption](docs/adoption.md)
219	
220	### Prior art
221	
222	Prior art is credited in full, including what was borrowed and from whom: [survey](docs/prior-art-frameworks.md) · [originality audit](docs/research/2026-07-10-originality-audit.md) · [comparative reviews](docs/research/2026-07-06-bmad-kiro-livespec-comparison.md), briefed to criticize all three subjects. This pack sits alongside BMAD, Kiro, and the wider spec-driven-development family. What it adds is the mechanical push gate and the recorded prover discipline. [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) is ahead of anything here on execution discipline, and its stars are earned. If you know prior art we missed, open an issue.
223	
224	**Known issues.** Internal vocabulary still leaks into human-facing text. A register lint — [`scripts/preshow-register-lint.py`](scripts/preshow-register-lint.py) — blocks the leaks it already knows before an artifact is shown, and chat stays the weakest surface. The spec still carries style debt, counted and capped in [`scripts/spec-debt-cap.json`](scripts/spec-debt-cap.json), with the work to clear it dated in the queue, [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md). The settings card is the page listing every setting the pack knows, its current value, and one plain line saying how to change it. That card is young and has run on one project. All three are tracked and reviewed at every push.
225	
226	One more, caught late. It is not yet in that tracking. This repository's own `guardrails.config.json` still carries the scaffold's placeholder `surface_discovery_pattern` (`<section id="...">`). That pattern matches nothing in plain markdown. So the reverse completeness direction — a rendered surface with no registry row — is inert here. What the push actually enforces is the forward direction: every row in [`SURFACES.md`](SURFACES.md) matching real content. Not yet fixed.

418:## The writing register — native open-source technical-writer voice
424:The **full register lives in [`references/writing-register.md`](references/writing-register.md)** — the
447:1. **Re-read the rules above, and the full writing register** — open this file and read the live text each
448:   time. Then open [`references/writing-register.md`](references/writing-register.md), the register's home

1	# The writing register — native open-source technical-writer voice
2	
3	Everything the pack writes for a human — spec prose, reports, decision cards, READMEs — reads in one
4	register: a native-English technical writer for a serious open-source project. Neutral, precise, easy
5	to follow. Never let it read as a marketing or pitch voice, a personal brand, or something quirky. (Defined 2026-07-07 after
6	the owner rejected both a "confident product pitch" draft and a persona-flavored one; his words, 2026-07-07:
7	write in the language of a native-speaker technical writer for open source, consistent and easy to read.) Seventeen rules:
8	
9	## Sentences and paragraphs
10	
11	How a single sentence and a single paragraph each carry one idea.
12	
13	- **One idea per sentence.** *(rule 1)* Target 15–25 words. A sentence carrying two clauses joined by a dash and a
14	   parenthetical gets split into two or three sentences.
15	- **One paragraph, one point.** *(rule 2)* State the point in the first sentence; the rest supports it. A reader
16	   who reads only first sentences still follows the section.
17	
18	## Terms
19	
20	How a specialized word is introduced and kept consistent.
21	
22	- **Define every abstract term in plain words at first use, then reuse it unchanged.** *(rule 3)* Picture first,
23	   term second: "Some parts of a project hold state — a screen, a panel, a saved file. The spec calls
24	   each of these a *stateful surface*." After that, always say "stateful surface".
25	- **A term is never bare on its debut.** *(rule 4)* "axis", "surface", "canonical axes", "provenance" met without
26	   a definition beside them is a defect. For a section readers may jump into directly, give a one-clause
27	   reminder or a pointer to the defining section.
28	- **One term per concept, everywhere.** *(rule 5)* If the defining section says "queue", every section says
29	   "queue". Never "roadmap", "backlog", or "the list" as a casual synonym. Synonym variety is a virtue
30	   in essays and a bug in a spec.
31	- **Prefer the concrete noun.** *(rule 6)* "A screen, a panel, a saved file" carries more than "an entity". When
32	   an abstraction is genuinely required, ground it with a two- or three-item example on first use, then
33	   use the abstraction alone.
34	
35	## Voice
36	
37	Who acts in the sentence, and which words a reader already knows.
38	
39	- **Active voice, named actor.** *(rule 7)* Say who does what: "the agent re-reads the file", "you approve the
40	   change", "the suite turns red". Passive voice is acceptable only when the actor is truly irrelevant.
41	- **Address the reader as "you"** *(rule 8)* for what a person does; name the component ("the installer", "the
42	   prover") for what software does. Never "one" or "the user is expected to".
43	- **Use words a reader recognizes without living in your head.** *(rule 13)*
44	    - Natural, well-understood industry
45	      language is good, even when it is a metaphor — "pipeline", "software house", "conveyor", "streamline",
46	      "ships" all land because a developer already holds them.
47	    - The words to avoid are invented internal
48	      terms and private interpretations: an abstraction that means something only inside this project.
49	    - When
50	      such a term is genuinely needed (for example "stateful surface" or "axis"), define it in plain words
51	      at first use (rule 3); after that it is safe to reuse.
52	    - The test: would someone outside the project
53	      recognize this word naturally? If yes, keep it. If it is your own coinage, define it or replace it.
54	
55	## Trim and shape
56	
57	Cut what adds nothing, and shape the whole into a readable structure.
58	
59	- **Examples earn their place by resolving ambiguity.** *(rule 9)* Add an example where a reader could read a rule
60	   two ways; cut examples that merely restate a clear rule. Use realistic values; one per rule is enough.
61	- **Cut nominalizations.** *(rule 10)* "Perform the reconciliation of" becomes "reconcile"; "the verification of
62	    the claim occurs" becomes "the suite verifies the claim". Verbs carry the meaning.
63	- **Cut throat-clearing and filler.** *(rule 11)* Delete "It is important to note that", "In practice",
64	    "Essentially", and intensifiers like "very", "actually", "of course". If deleting a phrase changes
65	    nothing, delete it.
66	- **Machine codes stay quiet and trailing.** *(rule 14)* The bracket anchors (`[INV-7]`, `[A-3]`, `[C-1]`) sit at
67	    the end of the sentence or clause they anchor. Prose never opens with a code or depends on one to be
68	    understood.
69	- **A document is a tree of grouped topics, never one flat list.** *(rule 16)*
70	    - Related rules or sections gather
71	      under a named parent that says what the group is about, so a reader meets the few big areas first
72	      and then the specifics under each.
73	    - A long flat run of peer items at one level is the smell to fix:
74	      gather them under two to five headed parents.
75	    - Levels nest without skipping — one document title,
76	      parts under it, topics under those, rarely deeper than three.
77	    - Every heading names its group's
78	      subject in a few plain words, so the outline alone tells a reader the document's shape.
79	    - A numbered
80	      item that stands as its own rule opens with a short bold title; a numbered item that is one step in
81	      a procedure ("read the size, then draft the delta, then queue it") stays a bare ordered list, since
82	      its order already carries the meaning. (2026-07-09: flat is the defect — structure the
83	      document, do more than label its items.)
84	
85	
86	## Framing
87	
88	Lead with what a thing is, and hold the contrast frame out.
89	
90	- **State rules positively.** *(rule 12)* Say what happens and when. Reserve negatives for genuine prohibitions
91	    ("never delete a host file"), stated as a plain imperative. The contrast frame is banned outright by
92	    rule 15.
93	- **Never the contrast frame — the hardest rule, and it holds in live chat too.** *(rule 15)* Never name a thing by
94	    denying its neighbour: stating what something is by pairing it with a denial of the alternative.
95	    - The
96	      shapes are an em-dash or a comma leading into the denied neighbour in English, and the parallel Russian
97	      constructions that set a negated word against the word meant to replace it.
98	    - This governs casual replies
99	      inside a running conversation as much as documents and artifacts; the human is allergic to the frame,
100	      and it stays absent even mid-dialogue.
101	    - Say what the thing IS in its own sentence. When a boundary
102	      genuinely needs naming, give it its own plain sentence: "The prototype is the norm. The prose describes
103	      it."
104	    - The ban holds even when the frame feels like the sharpest available phrasing; that pull toward it
105	      is the tell to rewrite.
106	    - The linter's scissors check holds the floor (`scripts/spec-style-lint.py`); the
107	      ceiling is a read-aloud that turns every denied-neighbour clause into its own positive sentence.
108	      (2026-07-09, restated with an explicit allergy: the frame stays out of chat replies to our
109	      conversations, and every earlier text carrying it is a bug to sweep.)
110	
111	
112	## Numbers
113	
114	What a number owes the reader who meets it.
115	
116	- **A number carries four things.** *(rule 17)* A number stated on its own is a defect.
117	    - **Why it is measured** — the decision it informs, or the question it answers.
118	    - **What changes when it moves** — what the project does differently if the number rises or falls.
119	    - **Its unit** — what is being counted, in what.
120	    - **Its method** — the command or the procedure that produced it, so a reader reproduces it.
121	    - The four stand in the number's own sentence or in the paragraph around it. A number quoted from a
122	      source the text names inherits that source's method.
123	    - No machine holds this rule. The scan that read a paragraph for a count whose method stood nowhere
124	      beside it was retired on 2026-08-17, and all four parts now rest where the other three already did:
125	      with a person or a reading model.
126	    - The case this rule rests on: a session reported that a reader returned a count of stops. That
127	      sentence named what a stop is, what the count decides, and how the count was produced, in none of
128	      its words. `DECISIONS.md` carries the owner's instruction of 2026-07-29 12:08.
129	
130	
131	**Verify each finished or edited piece of writing** — the checklist a good technical writer runs:
132	
133	1. **First-use check.** List every specialized term in the piece. Each is defined in plain words at
134	   first use here, or defined earlier with a reminder/pointer if this is a likely entry point.
135	2. **Cold-reader check.** Read it pretending you know nothing beyond the opening. Mark every sentence
136	   that only makes sense with prior system knowledge; each mark is a fix.
137	3. **Consistency grep.** For each key term, search the whole document for near-synonyms and drifting
138	   usage. One term per concept; fix strays at the source.
139	4. **Read-aloud test.** Read it aloud. Anywhere you stumble, run out of breath, or restart a sentence,
140	   rewrite that sentence.
141	5. **Actor check.** Every rule sentence answers "who does this, to what, when". Fix missing or hidden
142	   actors.
143	6. **Example audit.** Each example resolves a real ambiguity; each ambiguous rule has one.
144	7. **Deletion pass.** Try deleting each opener phrase, qualifier, and adjective. Keep only what changes
145	   meaning.
146	8. **Anchor integrity.** Every bracket code present before the edit is still present, still trailing,
147	   and still listed correctly in the project's generated code-to-location index. In this pack that
148	   index is `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md`, built from the body criteria at freeze. The hand-kept "Formal
149	   index" section it replaced was retired at the 4.0.0 format migration.
150	9. **Scissors scan (rule 15).** Before sending, scan the piece — chat replies to the human included — for
151	   the contrast frame in every shape: a denied-neighbour clause after an em dash or a comma, and its
152	   Russian equivalents that set a negated word against its replacement. Rewrite each hit into a positive
153	   sentence first. Run `scripts/spec-style-lint.py` for the mechanical floor; this scan runs on every
154	   message to the human, and on documents.
155	10. **Structure check (rule 16).** Read only the headings and the titles of numbered rules. They alone
156	    should reveal the document's shape — the few big areas and what groups under each. A long flat run of
157	    peer items with no parent grouping, a heading that hides its topic, or a skipped level is a fix.
158

1	# Prover records
2	
3	This directory holds one record per review pass. Every push carries exactly one of them, and that
4	one record does the whole job: it is the fresh re-check of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` and `ARCHITECTURE.md`
5	that the push gate has always demanded, and it is the adversarial read of the change the push is
6	about to send. The reviewer is briefed to find reasons the change should be refused, and holds the
7	change defective until evidence says otherwise. A read that sets out to confirm the change leaves
8	the requirement unmet.
9	
10	The rule lives in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` under `[M-6]`, `[INV-116]` and `[INV-304]`. The gate that reads
11	these records is `guardrails/check-prover-record.sh`, wired into `guardrails/pre-push` as gate a.
12	
13	Records of review passes that no push carries — a milestone re-prove, a periodic audit — live here
14	too, under the same file naming. Only a record written for a push owes the range fields below.
15	
16	## What the review covers
17	
18	The spec and the architecture as they now stand, and the delta being pushed: every commit between
19	the remote's head and the local head. Whatever is still uncommitted is read with them. The range
20	comes from the base ladder the gate walks — `LIVE_SPEC_DIFF_BASE`, then `origin/main`, then `HEAD~1`.
21	
22	The commit list for the record:
23	
24	```
25	git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
26	```
27	
28	## The record's shape
29	
30	One file per pass, named `YYYY-MM-DD[-slug].md`, committed before the push. The suffix is mandatory
31	once the date's plain file exists.
32	
33	```
34	# Prover record — 2026-08-05 <slug>
35	
36	PUSH-REVIEW
37	
38	Range: 258d544..9f21ab0
39	- 9f21ab0 <subject>
40	- 258d544 <subject>
41	Files read: PRODUCT_SPEC.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, guardrails/pre-push
42	Checks run: python3 -m pytest -q — 2,484 passed
43	Findings: <what the review found>
44	Blocking: none
45	```
46	
47	Those are all the fields, and the gate reads every one of them. Each carries a value. The commits
48	between the base and the head are listed under `Range:`, since the gate holds that the record names
49	every commit it covers. A review that found nothing writes into `Findings:` what it examined; the
50	absence then rests on the coverage the fields above state, rather than on silence.
51	
52	`Blocking:` reads `none`, or lists one item per blocking finding. Each item carries `closed:` with
53	what changed, or `stands:` with the reason it stands. A blocking finding holds the push until one of
54	those two is written.
55	
56	## What the gate holds, and what it leaves to the reviewer
57	
58	The gate holds:
59	
60	- a record dated today exists;
61	- the record is committed, rather than a scratch file in the working tree;
62	- the record is no older than the last change to `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` or `ARCHITECTURE.md`;
63	- the record is fresh against the pushed range;
64	- the record names the base commit and every reviewed commit;
65	- each field carries a value, and a blocking finding is closed or explained.
66	
67	The gate leaves three things to the reviewer:
68	
69	- whether the review was adversarial;
70	- whether the files the record names were read;
71	- whether the findings are the ones the delta deserved.
72	
73	No script decides those three. The record's named commits, files, checks and findings are the
74	pressure a machine can apply toward the review being real.

## Summary of the findings-gate repair

The coordinator flagged that `guardrails/check-doc-findings-bound.py` (gate aa) went red after the README layering work: README.md rose from its recorded 4 findings to 23 (20 sentences over the 25-word cap, plus 3 style-lint hits — one caps-shout on "AI", two accidental contrast-frame "scissors" constructions). Per the owner's clarified criterion, I fixed the **prose**, not the accounting: rewrote every flagged sentence (all introduced by the layering pass) into short, single-clause sentences that read in sequence without backtracking, cut filler intensifiers ("exactly", "honestly", "actually"), and removed the contrast-frame constructions — following `skills/communicator/references/writing-register.md` as the house rule. The four pre-existing long sentences (baseline, predating this work) were left untouched.

**Verified:** `rule-census.py README.md` now reads `4/0/0/4` (long/style/register/total), exactly matching the recorded baseline; `check-doc-findings-bound.py` is green (146 docs, none above record); `spec-style-lint.py --tier full` and `preshow-register-lint.py` are clean; SURFACES.md needles, the generated tree-counts block, and the host-count regex all still hold; 138 of the focused pytest suite passed (1 unrelated cross-process /tmp-leak teardown error on a shared, contended machine, not from this file). A quick single non-technical cold read of the top layer came back 0 blocking, 3 minor (all pre-existing or cosmetic, none introduced by this fix).
